lines.text: Korean five A, chapter seven: a successful life. In this episode we go through all 73 words of chapter seven, in the order of the word list.
For every word you hear the Korean, what it means, a tip, and a short example. Say the Korean out loud with us.
Next section: the video lesson. This section covers the words from the video lesson. They are about skill, habits, and doing things automatically without thinking.
An adjective meaning to be very skilled and smooth at handling something. It is a strong compliment for someone who works with ease and polish.
You hear it for skills like negotiating, public speaking or handling customers.
He is very skilled at negotiating.
An adverb describing doing things quickly and smoothly, without hesitation. It paints a picture of someone finishing tasks one after another.
Pair it with verbs like solving or finishing to praise someone's speed.
She got the work done smoothly.
An adjective meaning confident, dignified and not afraid to be seen. It has a positive feeling of standing tall with nothing to hide.
Don't mix it up with arrogant, because this word is admiring.
A noun meaning placing an order with a supplier. It is business language used between companies, not ordinary shopping.
It often appears in compounds, such as order volume, which is the amount you order.
An adverb used with a negative to mean not at all or not really. It carries a feeling of disappointment or dissatisfaction.
It must be followed by a negative, such as not liking something.
이 옷은 영 마음에 안 들어요.
I don't like these clothes at all.
An adjective meaning pathetic or pitiful, in a negative way. You use it when someone's behavior or situation makes you shake your head.
It is harsh, so avoid saying it directly to someone's face.
A verb meaning to connect, join or continue something so that it carries on. It can link two things, or carry on a line such as a tradition or a conversation.
Think of picking up a story right where the last person stopped.
I continued the conversation that had been cut off.
A noun form meaning everyday, ordinary or routine. It describes things that belong to normal daily life.
It usually comes before another noun, as in an everyday event.
A noun form meaning unconscious or done without thinking. It describes actions or habits that happen without a decision.
Typical for habits, like biting your nails without noticing.
I bit my nails without realizing it.
A noun for the parting line in your hair. Combined with the verb to take, it means to part your hair.
Remember that in Korean you take a parting, rather than make one.
I parted my hair on the right side.
A noun meaning automatic, something that works by itself. It is often attached to other nouns, like an automatic door.
Its opposite is doing things by hand.
A verb meaning to handle, process or deal with a task or problem. It sounds businesslike and is used for work, paperwork and trouble.
Use it for getting something taken care of, such as paperwork or complaints.
A noun meaning keyboard shortcut or hotkey. It is a key combination that does something fast on a computer.
It literally means shortened key, which makes it easy to remember.
Do you know the copy shortcut?
A noun meaning circuit, as in electronics. With the word for brain in front, it is used figuratively for the pathways of thinking.
Say brain circuit when you talk about how thought patterns are wired.
The circuits in my brain have changed.
An adverb meaning first of all or for now. You use it to say do this first and we'll see about the rest later.
It is a handy word to keep a conversation moving.
First, let's sit down and talk.
A noun meaning reward or compensation. It can be a prize for effort, or payment that makes up for a loss.
Context decides which one it is: a reward for effort or money for damage.
Effort is followed by a reward.
An informal expression meaning something is a piece of cake. Literally it says it is chewing gum, as in totally effortless.
It is casual slang for friends, not for your boss.
This much is a piece of cake.
A sharp rhetorical question meaning you call this a report? It is said by someone who thinks the work is far below standard.
Only a strict boss or an angry friend says this, so be careful.
Do you call this a report?
An expression meaning not particularly different. The speaker says there is little difference between two things.
It often appears in comparisons, like before and after.
퇴근 후의 모습도 별반 다르지 않네요.
How you look after work isn't much different either.
A grammar pattern meaning it looks like something unpleasant is about to happen. It attaches to a verb and warns of a likely, usually bad, outcome.
Mostly used for bad news, like being late or getting caught.
It looks like I'll be late again.
A grammar pattern meaning to do something on your own judgment, without being told. It carries the idea of handling it yourself, sensibly.
A boss who says do it as you see fit is using this idea.
It handles things automatically by itself.
Next section: reading one. These are the words from the first reading passage. It is about reading, opportunity, and widening your view.
A noun meaning opportunity or chance. It is positive, a moment you can use to your advantage.
You grab it or you miss it, so pair it with those verbs.
A noun for a bookworm, someone crazy about reading. The last part means maniac, so it is a bit stronger than just liking books.
Calling yourself this is a proud way to say you read a lot.
An expression meaning to stand out or show exceptional talent. Literally it means the tip of a horn shows, as if one horn rises above the crowd.
Use it for someone who shines in a field, like a student in math.
A noun meaning fear or dread. It is a feeling of being afraid, often of something uncertain or coming up.
It is the noun form of the verb meaning to be afraid.
A noun meaning preface or foreword, the introduction at the start of a book.
Literally it means head words, the words at the head of the book.
A noun meaning table of contents. It is the list of chapters at the front of a book.
Check it first to see whether a book covers your topic.
I chose it after looking at the table of contents.
A noun form meaning negative or pessimistic. It describes views, attitudes or effects that lean toward the bad side.
Its opposite is the positive form, and both attach to nouns with a particle.
A noun meaning loss or harm, usually financial or practical. It is what you suffer when things don't go in your favor.
It is often used with the verb meaning to see, as in taking a loss.
A noun meaning number or figure, as in digits and statistics.
Use it for numerals and statistics, as in the numbers don't lie.
An expression meaning to broaden your perspective. Literally it means to widen your point of view.
Reading and travel are the typical ways people do this.
I broadened my perspective through travel.
A noun meaning crisis or emergency, a dangerous turning point.
It is often paired with the verb meaning to overcome or to get through.
We got through the crisis well.
A noun meaning sincerity, your true and honest feelings.
Use it in the phrase meaning from the bottom of my heart.
A noun used like an adverb meaning to the maximum, or as much as possible.
Say it before a verb to mean do your utmost.
I'll come as fast as possible.
A verb meaning to be locked in or trapped. It is passive, so something has shut you in.
It can be literal, like an elevator, or figurative, like being trapped in old ideas.
I got trapped in the elevator.
A verb meaning to develop, such as a product, a skill or an area of land.
It is for creating or exploiting something new, not for growing up.
A verb meaning to respect or honor, especially someone's opinion or rights.
It is about valuing other people's views, a bit different from admiring someone.
A verb meaning to fill up or to complete something, like a glass or a quota.
It takes an object, so you are the one doing the filling.
I filled the cup with water.
An adjective meaning not far off, so soon or before long. It talks about a time that is near in the future.
It often shows up in an adverb form at the start of a sentence.
An adjective meaning to be no more than, or to amount to only. It stresses that something is smaller than you might think.
Use it to downplay a number, as in it is only that much.
An adverb meaning rather or on the contrary. It introduces a result that is the opposite of what you expected.
Use it when reality is the reverse of what someone assumed.
I helped him, but on the contrary he got angry.
An adverb meaning generously, without holding anything back.
It is often used for support, praise or giving.
Next section: reading two. These are the words from the second reading passage. They are about effort, focus, and getting results.
A noun meaning analysis, breaking something down to understand it.
Typical for data, results and causes.
A noun meaning weight, share or importance of something within a whole. With the verb to put, it means to give weight to something.
Think of putting weight on one side of a scale to show priority.
I give priority to my health.
A noun meaning result or achievement, especially a good outcome from work.
It leans positive, unlike a plain result that could be good or bad.
A word used as a noun or adverb meaning by oneself, on one's own initiative.
It stresses doing something without anybody pushing you.
A noun meaning an obstacle, a factor that stands in the way.
Common in reports about what blocks success.
A noun meaning intuition, understanding something directly without step by step reasoning.
People say they trust it when facts aren't enough.
A noun meaning use or application, making good use of something available.
It is also the grammar word for conjugation, so watch the context.
Make good use of the materials.
A verb meaning to tilt or lean something, and also to devote effort or attention to it.
To listen carefully, you tilt your ear toward the speaker.
A verb meaning to be immersed in something, totally absorbed.
Think of getting lost in a game or a book.
I was totally immersed in the book.
A verb with two meanings: to bury, and to ask. In the idiom, to bury one's bones means to commit yourself for life, to stay and give everything until you die.
The asking verb changes its ending sound when conjugated, while the burying one stays regular.
I work with the resolve to give my whole life to it.
A verb meaning to demonstrate or display an ability, bringing out what you have.
Use it with abilities such as talent, strength or leadership.
A verb meaning to take something as, or make something into. It sets one thing up as another, like a job or a friend.
Remember the structure: take A as B.
A verb meaning to clench your teeth. It also describes gritting your teeth to endure pain or push through.
It often appears in the sense of gritting your teeth and persevering.
I gritted my teeth and endured it.
A verb meaning to make an effort, to try hard.
It focuses on the struggle, even if the attempt doesn't succeed.
An adjective meaning unfamiliar or strange. Literally the face feels unfamiliar.
Use it for places, faces and feelings you aren't used to.
An adjective meaning enormous or tremendous, beyond what you would expect.
It works for good or bad things, because only the size matters.
Next section: speaking one. This section is for speaking. It gives you expressions and grammar patterns for stating and defending an opinion, quoting, emphasizing, and summarizing.
An expression for introducing your opinion: in my opinion. It is polite and fits both speech and writing.
It is a safe way to start an argument softly.
In my opinion this method is good.
Another way to say as I see it. It is a little more formal and makes clear that this is your own view.
Use it when you want to sound thoughtful in a discussion.
As I see it, it's too expensive.
A pattern for giving the reason behind your claim: the reason I think something is important is. It sets up your explanation.
Finish the sentence with a phrase that means because.
건강이 중요하다고 생각하는 이유는 행복 때문입니다.
The reason I think health is important is happiness.
은 는 다는 점에서 중요하다고 생각하다
A pattern meaning I think something is important in that it does or is a certain thing. The first part names the specific point.
Use it to give one concrete reason in a presentation.
독서는 시야를 넓힌다는 점에서 중요하다고 생각합니다.
I think reading is important in that it broadens our view.
은 는 다는 점에서 중요하다고 생각하다
A pattern for quoting a proverb: there is a saying that. The optional first word means in the old sayings.
It is great for opening a speech with a proverb.
There is an old saying that starting is half the battle.
A pattern for quoting someone: so and so said that. You put the quoted statement before the ending.
Use it to cite experts or famous people.
He said that effort is important.
A pattern meaning it is natural or inevitable that something happens. It states the normal course of things.
Think of it as things tend to turn out this way.
A pattern stating a universal truth, meaning it is the rule that. It describes what is generally expected to happen.
It is often used when comforting or lecturing with a life lesson.
It is the rule that hard work pays off.
An expression meaning based on my experience, literally in light of my experience. It supports your claim with your own past.
It is a good way to sound credible when giving advice.
제 경험에 비추어 볼 때 일찍 시작하는 게 좋아요.
Based on my experience, it is good to start early.
An expression meaning from my experience, a simpler version of the previous one.
제 경험으로 볼 때 그건 어려워요.
From my experience, that is difficult.
A grammar particle meaning the very one, precisely, or indeed. It marks the noun as the true example of something.
Attach it to a noun to say that this and nothing else is the real one.
Health, above all, is the most important.
A rhetorical question meaning isn't that so? It is formal and asks the listener to agree.
Use it at the end of an argument to draw in the audience.
A pattern meaning don't you think that. It is formal and polite, and invites the listener to agree.
It is stronger than a plain question, and often used in speeches.
Don't you think time is important?
지금까지 내용을 한마디로 요약하면 다는 것이다
A pattern for summing up: to summarize everything so far in one sentence, it is that. It signals your conclusion.
Say it right before your final point.
지금까지 내용을 한마디로 요약하면 노력이 중요하다는 것입니다.
To sum up everything so far in one sentence, effort is important.
지금까지 내용을 한마디로 요약하면 다는 것이다
A pattern for concluding: if we put together what has been said so far, it is that. It is more about combining several points.
Use it when you have gathered multiple points into one conclusion.
지금까지 이야기를 종합하면 계획이 필요하다는 것입니다.
Putting together what has been said so far, we need a plan.
That was every word of chapter seven. Play it again tomorrow, and try to say each Korean word before you hear it.
